subtopic: EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF TREASURY BOARD

speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (President of the Treasury Board):
subtopic: EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF TREASURY BOARD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the documents I have just tabled provide the details of the Government's expenditure plan for 1984-85. Last Wednesday, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) presented in his Budget the basic outlines of an updated expenditure plan for the next year through 1987-88. The documents tabled today elaborate on this overall plan for 1984-85 and on the policies, programs and activities underlying them. In particular, Part II and the related Part III documents, which together are generally known as the Main Estimates, provide detailed information on the major portion of the plan, that portion for which we are now seeking authorization from Parliament. Along with the Budget presented last week, the documents will provide a framework for conducting the business of government during the next year.

Mr. Speaker, the detailed plans in the Main Estimates for which we are seeking parliamentary authorization are the result of the government's intensive review of departmental programs over the last few months. They take into account the assumptions about economic conditions that were presented last week by my colleague, the minister of Finance.

Before touching upon some of the highlights of the detailed expenditure plans for next year, I would like to comment briefly on the documents themselves which are presented again this year as a group of volumes-Part I, the Government expenditure plan itself; Part II, the Main Estimates proper or the blue book; and Part III, departmental expenditure plans. [Translation]
In its fourth annual edition, Part I is becoming firmly established in parliamentary tradition, providing us with an overview of federal government spending. It deals with the broad policy areas to which resources will be allocated by the Government, and is aimed at facilitating an overall understanding of government expenditures.

While the focus of this overview is on 1984-85, information is provided on the full multi-year expenditure plan through to 1987-88 presented in last week's Budget. This represents a return to the practice of previous years from the single-year focus of last year's Part I, which was in that form because it was presented before the Budget of April, 1983 which contained this multi-year information.
I have tabled on behalf of my colleagues 65 volumes of Part III for 1984-85, adding 18 new plans to the 47 tabled last year. Next year, when Part III will be complete, departmental expenditure plans will be available for all Departments and agencies. These documents are prepared by individual Departments and agencies with guidance from the Office of the Comptroller General. They contain a wealth of information on government programs; most important, they outline what the Government expects to achieve with the money it plans to spend once the Estimates are approved. The blue book, Part II, supports the items which are expected to be included in the Appropriation Act for the Main Estimates.
I would now like to comment upon the details of the Government's expenditure plan contained in the documents just tabled. Members will, of course, be familiar with the basic outlines of the updated multi-year expenditure plan set out in Part I, since they were presented to Parliament only last week by the Minister of Finance. They will recall that he forecast for 1984-85 planned total outlays of $98.2 billion, an increase of 8.3 per cent over his revised forecast of $90.6 billion for 1983-84. I would draw to the attention of the House the fact that this is the lowest rate of growth of total outlays in six years. I would also note that the Minister of Finance has projected in his Budget even lower rates of growth for total outlays for the next three years. These lower rates of growth
February 21, 1984

reflect both our current economic recovery, which is removing pressures from some of our major income support programs, and more optimistic forecasts for inflation.
Within our total outlays, total planned expenditures of $98.2 billion for 1984-85, we are at this time seeking authorization from Parliament to spend amounts totalling $96.5 billion which are detailed in the Main Estimates; that is to say, the blue book and the related Part III documents. This total is
10.4	per cent higher than the 1983-84 Main Estimates total. This represents a substantial decrease compared with last year's 17.9 per cent increase over the 1982-83 Main Estimates. [Translation]
Mr. Speaker, beyond the expenditure total for which details are provided in the Main Estimates, our overall Expenditure Plan also includes $3.1 billion in reserves which are allocated across various policy sectors or envelopes, and a special reserve of $800 million to cover any necessary adjustments to current forecasts for statutory programs. The envelope reserves serve two purposes. The first is to cover the costs of planned initiatives that have not been included in the Main Estimates, that is to say the increases to the Youth Opportunity Fund and the Guaranteed Income Supplement for single pensioners announced in the Budget, as well as other initiatives on which final decisions have not yet been taken by Cabinet. The second is to cover cost adjustments to existing programs that could not be anticipated at the time the Main Estimates were being prepared. In either instance, parliamentary approval will, of course, be sought through Supplementary Estimates or other legislation.

Our planned total outlays of $98.2 billion are exclusive of, are net of, two items which total $2.2 billion. The first of these is to account for forecast repayments on loans issued in previous years. The second is an adjustment to account for the fact that some authorized expenditures will not be made and will lapse since Departments and agencies cannot legally spend more money than Parliament authorizes and in fact always spend less.
I would now like to direct the attention of the House again to the $96.5 billion in expenditures provided for in the Main Estimates. I would first note that $2 billion of this total is for loans, investments and advances. Of the remaining amount, eight items account for two-thirds of the $8.9 billion increase over 1983-84 Main Estimates. National Defence expenditures are up $927 million to meet Canada's commitment to NATO to increase the real growth of defence expenditures by 3 per cent annually. A large part of these funds will be devoted to the re-equipment and modernization of the Canadian Forces, including the CF-18 fighter aircraft and Canadian-built patrol frigate programs. These activities will also provide stimulus to key sectors of the Canadian economy.
Second, there are the transfers to the provinces under the Established Programs Financing arrangements which support
Main Estimates, 1984-85
the financing of health care and post-secondary education. These are up by $886 million compared to last year's Main Estimates. Of course, apart from and not included in last year's Main Estimates are the special payments of more than $500 million announced by the Government in December, resulting from revisions to the national income and expenditure accounts by Statistics Canada.
Transfers to the provinces under the Canada Assistance Plan are up by $556 million. Payments under the Petroleum Incentives Program, made primarily to Canadian oil companies to support oil and gas exploration and development, show an increase of $450 million. Payments under this program contribute to the overall level of economic activity, particularly in the natural resource sector. Also, the Old Age Security payments, guaranteed income supplement and spouses' allowances are up by a total of $430 million.
In addition to this amount, more funds will be required as a result of the announcement in last week's Budget of the substantial increase in the guaranteed income supplement for single pensioners. Parliament will be asked to approve this increase through legislation soon to be introduced by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin).
There are also transfers to the provinces, primarily in the form of equalization payments, which are up by $339 million. There are two payments to Canada Post, one for $350 million pursuant to the Canada Post Corporation Act to cover operating requirements and one for $170 million to provide for capital costs associated with the mailing of certain Canadian publications. These are included in this year's Main Estimates. The payments have until now been presented in supplementary estimates.
Public debt charges account for $1.8 billion of the increase. This increase will result from higher debt levels that are partially offset by lower average interest rates on the outstanding debt. The Minister of Finance pointed out last week that the deficits leading to higher debt levels have come from additional expenditures to assist individual Canadians and to promote job creation and economic activity generally, through the difficult period of the recession and the beginning stages of recovery. With recovery well under way and investment activity on the increase, the Minister of Finance last week reiterated the Government's commitment to bring the deficit down, but in a phased manner that does not damage our economic prospects.

Mr. Speaker, I would remind Hon. Members that the Estimates documents and related press material contain a wealth of information on these and many other changes. Therefore, I now would like to describe how the continuing economic recovery, and this government's initiatives in support of that recovery, have very profoundly affected today's Main Estimates and the government's Expenditure Plan.

I want to deal briefly with four areas in particular: Special Recovery Capital Projects, unemployment insurance, Estab-

February 21, 1984
Main Estimates, 1984-85
lished Programs Financing and the guaranteed income supplement.
1 mentioned earlier that eight items account for two-thirds of the year-over-year increase in budgetary Main Estimates. Of the remaining $3 billion increase this year, about one-third is for Special Recovery Capital Projects. These are aimed at accelerating federal spending on economic infrastructure projects to facilitate Canada's economic recovery. These are part of the Special Recovery Program announced in the April, 1983 Budget and which the Minister of Finance pointed to again last week as a key link in the Government's efforts toward establishing partnership in the establishing of jobs through a healthy and growing economy. Excluding national defence spending and expenditures on these Special Recovery Capital Projects, the operating and capital expenditures of Departments and agencies are increasing in the order of only 7 per cent.
Last year, as we were just beginning to recover from the recession, we faced a very sharp increase in the Government's contribution to unemployment insurance. I am pleased to note that, based on economic forecasts, this year's Main Estimates figure of $2.7 billion is $227 million less than last year's Main Estimates forecast figure, a reflection of our improving economic circumstances and of improvements in the level of employment in particular.
Under the Established Programs Financing arrangements, the federal Government defrays approximately half the cost of financing hospital insurance and medicare and slightly more than half the cost of financing post-secondary education. This contribution takes the form of cash payments to the provinces and of the value of the potential to exact taxes which is turned over to them by the federal Government. An increase in the value of this tax portion is automatically offset by a decrease in the federal Government's cash contributions under the formula set out in the Act.
The total to which the provinces are entitled for 1984-85 is expected now to increase by 8.4 per cent over the current forecast for 1983-84, exclusive of adjustments for prior years. However, the value of the tax portion is expected to increase by more than 13 per cent, so that the cash portion need only grow by 4 per cent. This is indeed a welcome sign of increasing economic health and is a direct analogue of the healthier growth in budgetary revenues indicated in the fiscal plan tabled last week by the Minister of Finance.
I also wish to review briefly forecast expenditures under major income support programs for the elderly, as reflected in the Main Estimates. Old Age Security payments are made to all Canadians over the age of 65. The guaranteed income supplement is paid to those Canadians receiving Old Age Security who qualify on the basis of an income test. These payments are normally indexed to the growth in the consumer price index. Under our six and five program, however, the indexation of Old Age Security payments was limited to 6 per cent in 1983 and 5 per cent in 1984.
This limitation did not apply to the guaranteed income supplement, which indeed not only continued to be fully
indexed but was modified to compensate its recipients should there be any loss of income resulting from the limit placed on the indexation of Old Age Security. Last year's forecast of expenditures for the guaranteed income supplement assumed indexation rates for inflation in excess of the six and five limit and also included a provision to offset the capping of indexation for eligible Old Age Security recipients.
We should all be pleased that the assumptions about inflation turned out to be higher than the rates actually achieved through the efforts of all of us working together to reduce inflation. This means, of course, that all the funds set aside for the reasons I have just explained were not needed; but more importantly, it illustrates in a tangible way the success we have had in reducing inflation through our co-operative efforts. These factors also explain why the 1984-85 Main Estimates forecast of expenditures for the guaranteed income supplement is actually lower than the 1983-84 Main Estimates forecast. [Translation]
I would also note that for the first time in many years, expenditures related to major transfer programs like unemployment insurance are growing more slowly than total spending this year. Again, this is largely due to improving economic conditions.

Before completing my remark, I would like to speak briefly about the size of the public service as measured by the number of person-years under the direct control of the Treasury Board. The Main Estimates documents before the House indicate a 1984-85 total of 260,370 person-years for Departments and agencies whose personnel requirements are controlled by the Treasury Board. This represents an increase of only 1 per cent over the comparable 1983-84 Main Estimates level of 257,678. This latter number, I would remind Members, includes the reduction in authorized levels made by the Treasury Board just prior to the tabling of the Main Estimates last February but which, as a result, did not show in last year's blue book.
The limited increases in authorized person-years reflect the commitment of this Government to continuing restraint in the growth of the Public Service, and to ongoing efforts to achieve improved productivity in the delivery of services to the public.
If we analyse the areas where the larger increases occur, the Government's interest in maintaining and increasing services to the public becomes apparent. The person-year level of Revenue Canada Taxation will increase by 1,044 over 1983-84 to provide enhanced services to the public. The additional personnel will be allocated entirely to four activities: about 17 per cent to handling telephone and over-the-counter inquiries from the public for tax information, 53 per cent for processing tax returns, 15 per cent for tax adjustments requested by taxpayers, and 15 per cent for dealing with formal appeals of assessment registered by taxpayers. These additional resources will be allocated to all regions of the country. No additional person-years have been approved for audit, enforcement, collection or administration. As a complement to these increases
February 21, 1984

in human resources, financial resources are being made available to improve telephone and computer facilities so that services can be provided more rapidly and more effectively to the public.
The Correctional Services program has had its authorized level increased by 666, primarily because of growth in the number of penitentiary inmates. The Department of Transport levels are up by 403, largely to provide for regulatory activities related to air safety and to meet staffing requirements for the Canadian Coast Guard fleet. While maintaining and even increasing services to the public generally, it has still been possible to reduce person-year resources in some areas; the number of authorized person-years is down for 22 departments and agencies. For example, authorized levels for the RCMP have been reduced by 175 person-years because of decreased demand for police services from provinces and municipalities. While some of the decrease of 158 person-years shown for the Department of Veterans Affairs reflects the phasing out of temporary requirements related to the relocation to Charlottetown, a part of the reduction is being made possible by the installation of a modern, computerized benefit delivery system.
The documents tabled today reflect some of the ongoing benefits already being gained through programs related to improving the productivity of government operations. I am referring in particular to the IMPAC program, which deals with improving management practices and controls. This program, which is being gradually extended across the Government, is already providing annual recurring savings of $122 million. The documents cannot at this early stage, however, reflect the positive results we expect to flow from the four point plan of new initiatives aimed at further improving productivity in the operation of the federal public sector which I announced a few weeks ago.

Mr. Speaker, the Expenditure Plan documents that I have tabled also illustrate the achievements and efforts related to building a strong and growing economy to which my colleague, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde), drew our attention in his Budget statement last week. You will recall that he pointed to the significant reduction in inflation that has been achieved; the measures taken to secure economic recovery; the record on economic growth, employment and inflation over the last ten months, which has been consistently better than forecast in his previous Budget; and the need for a strategy of continued effort aimed at creating jobs through partnership with the private sector.

On its side of the partnership the Government is making a major contribution through such initiatives as the $1 billion Youth Opportunity Fund, which was announced in the Speech from the Throne and to which the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) added $150 million in his Budget of last week. In all, funds already allocated to Special Recovery Capital Projects and to the direct support of employment, including job training, will total over $3.5 billion in 1984-85.
Main Estimates, 1984-85
I will conclude by saying that I am pleased to table these documents relating to our detailed expenditure plan for next year. I believe they illustrate graphically our success in managing and planning our expenditures in this still difficult economic period, although it is one of growing economic recovery. They also reflect the well founded optimism this Government shares with the private sector that Canada will continue its progress toward a healthy and growing economy.

subtopic: EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF TREASURY BOARD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have had two major statements of policy from the Government, the budget speech on February 15 and now the tabling of the Main Estimates for 1984-85 by the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Gray).
Pray, Mr. Speaker, that the rhetoric in these two documents will deliver 10 per cent of the optimism it expresses about bringing the Canadian economy around to a condition of full employment or at least from 3 per cent to 7 per cent unemployment, and pray that the rhetoric will become fact. I have to say to you, Mr. Speaker, and to others who are listening-

subtopic: EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF TREASURY BOARD
speechtext: Nobody is listening.

subtopic: EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF TREASURY BOARD
speechtext:
That is absolutely true. No one on the government side of the House listens to anything at any time. The House of Commons, both at Westminster and in this country, was born out of violence, debate, sword lengths and so on. The manner in which the President of the Treasury Board handled his Estimates today is a great improvement over what we have had in the last three or four years. At one time our colleague, the Hon. Member for York-Peel (Mr. Stevens), almost had to join the Press Gallery in order to get to a briefing session before the Estimates were tabled. Today we were told by the President of the Treasury Board that we have 67 documents that you and I, Mr. Speaker, did a lot to bring about in our days as members of the Public Accounts Committee. There are 67 documents in Part III, the Main Estimates, which are a considerable size, and then we have Part I. All of that is coming to pass as some of us in the thirtieth Parliament had hoped. I congratulate the President of the Treasury Board on the furthering of the effort that started with a parliamentary committee. I congratulate him on the courtesy he extended to the Official Opposition and the other Party in opposition for a briefing which began at 12 noon today on this matter. I do not want to go beyond that in thanks and congratulations, however; that is about as good as I am going to go in the department.
The total estimate of expenditures announced in the speech today is $96.5 billion. The forecast expenditure shows a 10.4 per cent increase in a comparison of the 1984-85 Estimates with the 1983-84 Estimates. The rhetoric will say that this increase has been brought down to 8.3 per cent when the 1983-84 supplements are included. That is correct, after the adjustments are made.
In the 1979 Crosbie Budget there was a prediction that in 1983-84 we would spend $77.7 billion; the Liberal forecast is for the spending of $90.65 billion, which is 16 per cent higher

February 21, 1984
Main Estimates, 1984-85
than the projection by the same staff in 1979. We have a forecast to prediction problem in all governments, not just ours. It is a problem we are all going to have to live with. The system is too complicated and the factors of input are so complicated that there is a very high percentage of error in the projections. That is something we must all recognize and wrestle with.
In November, 1981, the spending projections for the 198485 year were $93.9 billion; in fact they turned out to be $4.3 billion more. It is interesting that in the rhetoric we have heard from the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) and from the President of the Treasury Board, the Government claims that it cannot control most spending because it is non-discretionary.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
subtopic: EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF TREASURY BOARD
speechtext: That's right.

subtopic: EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF TREASURY BOARD
speechtext: That is right, is it? Let us listen to the next line, then. When we compare discretionary spending in these Estimates against non-discretionary spending, we see that the discretionary spending goes up 13.2 per cent and the non-discretionary goes up 8.8 per cent. So there is something wrong with the rhetoric of the Minister of Finance and the President of the Treasury Board. The facts show that it is not so.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
subtopic: EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF TREASURY BOARD
speechtext: The Special Recovery Program.

subtopic: EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF TREASURY BOARD
speechtext:
The Special Recovery Program? There is always something, Mr. Speaker. These Estimates signal, Sir, a total disregard for the hardship presently faced by Canadians. Let us measure the gap between what the Government says and what it actually does. I suggest that the Government should not be judged in the narrow sense of output, in terms of the services it provides or does not provide. Government should be judged according to the outcome and how well it overcomes the circumstances which shape the results. On the basis of today's Estimates, Sir, last week's Budget and the promises made to entice voters mean little. Government only proposes to throw more and more money at the nation's problems.
Every time we turn a radio on or watch TV we hear something about a make-work program. We heard again today about a $150 million Youth Opportunity Fund. Why would this $150 million be delivered to Canada Works? If it were delivered to Career Access, two and a half times more jobs per dollar would be created than under these Canada Works programs. Why can we not rearrange some of this spending whereby we would get the optimum multiplier in terms of relieving the pressure on the people who are seeking work? Today we Find out that in the Economic Development Ministry 33 person-years have been added. This envelope ministry has now taken on the responsibilities of a line department. It has taken on the responsibilities of a line department because it is now operating the Gaspe and the lower St. Lawrence Special Recovery Capital Projects. I am surprised to see that in this set of documents. Why has the responsibility not been left to the line departments? Why must this politically sensitive central agency function beyond and outside of its mandate? I believe we should have a reply to that.
Too little money did not move Canada from sixth place to twenty-second place among industrial nations in one year, Mr. Speaker. Our ailments in efficiency, which have reduced us to fifteenth place among industrialized nations, will not be cured with more money. The productivity performance of Canada is dismal, and we are now going to have another commission or set up another bureau to study our productivity problems when most of us know exactly what the problem is.
On the industrial scene, the pace of improvement is the slowest of that of any major industrialized nation. Those figures come for the Euromoney study, Sir. In 1982, productivity in Canada declined by 2.8 per cent. Yet we find the Minister of State for Economic Development (Mr. Johnston) now moving into highly politicized areas instead of really planning what has to happen down the road in terms of major fundamental corrections to our system. We talk about productivity. We set up a bureau to study it. At the same time we have seen a doubling in the number of notices of objections received by Revenue Canada since 1979. In 1984-85 it expects to process over 56,400 objections. How can one talk about productivity, Sir, when we have a tax collector who is doing all he can to destroy the entrepreneurial private sector with this kind of intervention. If we are going to talk about productivity, we must get the political rhetoric out of it. We must address the fundamental problems which this Government has caused in the private sector, the same private sector on which it is now relying to save us all from a worse recession. Revenue Canada will require 6 per cent more staff in district offices and in its head office just to handle this new workload which it has created for itself. This is going to increase its personnel costs by 10.2 per cent at the same time that the Government talks about productivity.
At page 15290 of Hansard of February, 1982, the then President of the Treasury Board said that the improved presentation of the Estimates to Parliament would help Members of Parliament to ensure that taxes paid by Canadians would be used for the benefit of all Canadians. One cannot object to that kind of rhetoric, Sir. He said that this was a fundamental and democratic responsibility. But the Estimates which have been tabled today are in the shadow of an enormous porkbar-rel out of which huge sums of money are flowing to the benefit and advantage of Liberal candidates in the next election. We heard rhetoric back in 1982 and we receive a set of Estimates today in the shadow of behaviour which I do not believe I have seen in my lifetime in this country.
I agree, Sir, with the Minister of Transport (Mr. Axworthy) who indicated last night on The Journal that he had reservations about the priorities and conduct of his colleagues who are preparing to lead the Liberal Party. But the Minister of Transport, who has been headlined in the paper as one certainly able to lasso loot, Sir, while we are talking about austerity and care of public funds hands out chronicles of his achievements. He publishes them. There was $1.3 million that went to the Max Bell Athletic Complex at the University of Manitoba. However, that Minister allowed $31,000 of that money to go to a consultant in the United States when the best consultants
February 21, 1984

in the world on that subject matter are right here in Canada. There was $10.2 million for a maintenance hangar for Air Canada in Winnipeg; a $32 million facelift for the Winnipeg airport; $4 million went for a vocational training centre; $50,000 was spent to avert lay-offs of two individuals at the symphony; $115,000 went to the blind to learn computer programming; $55,000 was given to the Fort Garry Women's Centre; $8 million went to CMHC; $100,000 went to Canada Ports for an audit contract in Winnipeg. The Canada Ports audit is now being conducted out of Winnipeg. There was $90,000 spent for experimental buses for the aged. All that was spent in his constituency.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
subtopic: EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF TREASURY BOARD
speechtext: More.

subtopic: EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF TREASURY BOARD
speechtext:
I hear them calling for more over there, Mr. Speaker. I want to tell you, Sir, that that kind of behaviour is irresponsible when one keeps talking about equity and fairness in the Canadian system. It is not equity and fairness; it is grab what you can. The headline says, Sir, "Lloyd lassos federal loot". There never was a guy who could throw a lasso like that Hon. Minister.
At page 23101 of Hansard of last year, the President of the Treasury Board said that the federal Government must be able to adapt to the circumstances and have the flexibility to review and revise its programs so as to promote economic recovery. Where, Sir, in the documents which the President of the Treasury Board tabled today is the inflation rate? The Government brags about the fact that it has gone down to 5.3 per cent. It was under 5 per cent two months ago. It is now up to 5.3 per cent. But where is the inflation rate reflected in reduced government expenditures, Sir? Why is the largest Borrowing Authority Bill presented to Parliament crowding out the availability of capital to private borrowers? The Government wants to borrow $29.5 billion. That Bill just came in the last day of last week. How can the private sector accept the job-creation challenge the Liberal Government has given it before interest rates come down and we have some degree of stability? While we have all this rhetoric, we also have the Minister of Finance advertising non-callable 21 year bonds, that is until the year 2005, at 12 per cent. The projection for interest rates in the United States as a result of their recovery is dropping year by year to the point where 91 day Treasury bills are expected to be 5 per cent in the year 1989. Yet here we are going through to the year 2005 at 12 per cent and sucking all the money we can out of the private sector. At the same time we expect that private sector to deliver the recovery and put Canadians back to work. It is an exercise in conflict, Sir. You can hardly believe what is going on.
As both you and I know, Mr. Speaker, bankruptcies have doubled this year compared with the first seven months of 1979. Some 6,122 businesses went bankrupt in the first seven months of 1983. Yet the Government expects the private sector to invest in new and more modern plants to increase productivity, create jobs and allow us to be competitive once again in world markets. It is not realistic when compared with
Main Estimates, 1984-85
what is happening in Asia and the U.S. We are completely out of touch.
Since taking office in 1980, Government expenditures have increased 13 per cent in 1980-81, 17.6 per cent in 1981-82, 17.8 per cent in 1982-83, approximately 12 per cent in 198384, and now, comparing the Main Estimates, 10.4 per cent between 1983-84 and 1984-85, which can be corrected down to
8.4	per cent. The Government is very proud of its 8.4 per cent but it does not hear the warnings from knowledgeable people.
Through you, Mr. Speaker, I would like to speak as directly as I can to the President of the Treasury Board. I have been told by very responsible researchers in world economics that we will not have a recovery in Canada until we start to see our primary resources, such as zinc, copper, steel, molybdenum and lead, along with wood and food, start moving out to world markets. We have priced ourselves out of world markets, and there are so many political rigidities in our system which we are terrified to touch that we are going to have great trouble getting back on track in the next decade. I hear the rhetoric from the Minister of Finance and the President of the Treasury Board, but if we are going to be realistic and face the real problems of the real world instead of this wonderland in Ottawa, Sir, we have to change these attitudes and get down on our knees and address some very fundamental factors. If we cannot put people to work and paying taxes, where is the future? It is not in the rhetoric of the Minister of Finance and of the President of the Treasury Board.
The challenges which lie ahead for whatever Party forms the next government are truly brutal. If we are going to save the social programs and everything else we are so proud of in this country, we will have to become very realistic. People are absolutely aghast at the practices of Revenue Canada, the way they are treating taxpayers and making retroactive reassessments. We all have problems, not just the Government. Private individuals are having real problems, too.
Then we have this matter of Government advertising and the waste involved, which develops a real anger in people. For instance, the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. De Bane) is spending $2 million to promote the eating of fish. If he could spend that money promoting the quality of fish harvesting, processing and packaging, it would be of lasting benefit down the road. It is very interesting that in this set of Estimates advertising is no longer shown. Last year it was shown in the Supply and Services revolving fund. But the Government removed it and again started playing this shell game with the figures. Information as an object of expenditure in the 1983-84 Main Estimates was $244.6 million. The 1983-84 update was $269.1 million, a difference of $24.5 million in advertising. The Estimates for 1984-85 show total information expenditures of $266.2 million. On the surface that is a reduction from last year's revised $266 million, but on the basis of a comparison of main estimates, it is up 9 per cent. However, if you include the advertising normally reported in the main estimates and the supplementary estimates, if you include the Crown corporations, I am told unofficially that it is over $1 billion. If the President of the Treasury Board has information

February 21, 1984
Main Estimates, 1984-85
to refute that claim, Sir, I would like him to deliver it to us in the Elouse of Commons.
We have a lot of problems, Sir, and I have many other examples.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subtopic: EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF TREASURY BOARD
speechtext: I hesitate to interrupt the Hon. Member but he has been given equal time with the Minister. He could be allowed to continue with the unanimous consent of the House. Is that agreed?

subtopic: EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF TREASURY BOARD
speechtext: Agreed.

subtopic: EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF TREASURY BOARD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the Minister and my colleagues. I note that under the office of the Co-ordinator for the Status of Women, the scientific and professional personnel authorized person-years have been cut from ten to six. These are the people who put together the real facts and issues, and they have been cut back, but the overall person-years are up by seven. Here they cut an essential element from ten to six, a saving of four person-years, and yet the overall person-years are up by seven. The Estimates indicate that the increase is mainly due to the expansion of the public information functions. This is more advertising for the operations of the Secretary of State's office. If you will refer to fact sheet No. 4 in the documents tabled today, you will find that the information budget rises from $33,000 to $252,000 this year in the sector and the salaries and wages are up 20.9 per cent. In that area, where they get real value for money, they cut.
I cannot conclude without mentioning the condition of Mirabel, that monument to the East, that mecca of productivity and efficiency. Through the Estimates we are told that Mirabel is to lose $48.2 million in the year ahead. This loss will be up from $43.9 million, the actual loss experienced this year. May I remind you, Sir, that in 1982-83 the loss of only $29.2 million on that marvellous installation.
At the beginning of my comments I complimented the President of the Treasury Board on two things. I complimented him on the courtesy he extended to his colleagues in the House of Commons by giving us a briefing period before the tabling of the Estimates. I sincerely thank him for that. The other thing I thank him for is that he has continued to work on the reform of the Estimates with some energy, push and drive in laying the foundation of which the Speaker of the House of Commons, when he was co-chairman of the Standing Committee on Public Accounts, along with myself, worked so hard. If we examine the summary tables and the gobal figures in Part I of the Estimates and the Main Estimates we can see that none of this is going to work unless we pay attention to the Special Committee on Standing Orders and Procedure which was struck and worked for 18 to 20 months and brought down a series of 10 reports. We cannot think that the building of bureaucracies is going to remove from us, the elected representatives of the people, the responsibility of holding the federal Government to account. We in the Opposition are responsible for holding the Government to political account for political misdemeanour and misbehaviour. We in the House
are also responsible for holding the bureaucracy to account when it is not delivering full value for money in the management of the resources voted to serve the objectives that the Government brings down.
I urge Hon. Members to read and reread Chapter 2 of the Auditor General's report. If we are going to serve the people of the country properly and address the rigidities that we have to address, before we can really turn this country around and have a private sector that can start employing people again we will have to accept report No. 7 and allow the House of Commons the muscle, material and organization to hold the Government to account. I do not care whether the Government is them or us. We have also got to learn to hold the bureaucracy, the managers of the system, to value for money accountability in terms of the way they manage the resource in service of the political objectives and programs laid down by the Government in power.
That is the challenge we have here. There is no political will among Members in the House of Commons to bring it about. We all think we get here by being big spenders. That is all we are. We shovel money, promises and rhetoric out and will not face the essential rigidities that we have built into our system. Until we do, through the committee structure in report No. 7, I think we are in for very serious times indeed. It is time for Members in the House of Commons to show leadership, hold the Government to better account and hold the bureaucracy to account under value for money principles.
I thank my colleagues in the House for having allowed me these few minutes to continue my remarks.

subtopic: EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF TREASURY BOARD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in commencing the few words I have to say about the tabling of the Estimates and the documents which were tabled today in the House by the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Gray), I would like to agree with the Hon. Member for Capilano (Mr. Huntington) that there has been a great deal of change in the Estimates since I arrived here about four years ago. When I first arrived in Ottawa all we had to go through in the Estimates was the blue book. Now we have added other parts to the Estimates. There is a government expenditure plan and departmental expenditure plans which are very helpful. There is still a great deal of difficulty in gleaning the information one actually needs to make comparisons from year to year in the Estimates and tie it to the public accounts of Canada. I will go on to say more about that later.
One of the first things which struck me as I attended the briefing session today, which started at twelve o'clock, was the number of person-years which were increased in some of the departments and agencies. The largest increase in person-years of employment within the federal Government occurred in Revenue Canada Taxation. There are 1,044 increased person-years, supposedly for the benefit of the Canadian taxpayer. I wonder whether there is a direct correlation with one of the other highest increases in person-years of employment. In Correctional Services there is an increase of 662 person-years of employment. I certainly hope there is not a direct correla-
February 21, 1984

tion and that we will find Revenue Canada being even more strict with the Canadian taxpayers.
As in the Budget, Mr. Speaker, these Estimates do not deal with the unemployment and job security of Canadians. I am a little distressed by that. The Minister is very proud of the fact that the unemployment insurance contributions by the federal Government will decrease from $2.8 billion last year to $2.6 billion this year. The Budget is a more recent document than these Estimates because of the way they are prepared. The Budget says that the decrease is actually down to $2.7 billion.
You must look at this very carefully, Mr. Speaker. This does not mean that unemployment is going down in Canada. In fact it means, as I will try to point out, that the problem of unemployment is being transferred from the federal Government to the provincial governments across the country. If you compare the unemployment insurance contributions by the federal Government to the Canadian Assistance Plan, you will find that the contributions which the federal Government makes to that will go up by 17.7 per cent or, in terms of dollars, a $556 million increase that the federal Government will have to pay in Canada Assistance Plan payments to the provincial governments. It should be remembered that this is a cost shared program. It only reflects half the real cost of people who are unemployed in the country and have gone beyond receiving unemployment to the point of dependency on welfare without much prospect of obtaining jobs in the future.
The Minister is actually saying that the program of unemployment insurance, which is a 100 per cent federal responsibility, is going down. But actually it is not, because when you compare that to the cost-shared program of the Canada Assistance Plan, which goes to welfare payments which the provinces distribute, it actually means that unemployment is much worse in the country. We cannot rely on statistics alone. We have to look at the real unemployment problem in the country. That means that more and more people are not only unemployed, but have lost hope for employment and are reduced to the bleak prospect of having to receive welfare to keep food on their tables and shelter over their heads.
These Estimates refer to the $600 million for job creation for youth. By the Government's own admission, that program would employ about 40,000 young people. The fact remains that there are some 540,000 young people unemployed in the country today. That amount will hardly put a dent in it at all.
When I talked about the Estimates being clearer than I have seen them in the four years I have been here, I must note that it is still quite difficult to determine the actual information in terms of the estimates and expenditures of the Government. Let me give one example. Again, it concerns the pressing problem of job security and unemployment for many Canadians. The Minister seems quite proud of the fact that there is an increase of $134 million for direct job creation, particularly for Canada Works and career access programs. However, these facts require closer study because the Government, in its background papers, has compared the 1983-84 Estimates with
Main Estimates, 1984-85
the 1984-85 Estimates which have just been tabled in the House. While that comparison shows that there is $ 134 million more for contributions toward direct job creation, a closer examination reveals otherwise. One year's estimates cannot simply be compared with the next year's estimates, because there are other items such as supplementary estimates and additional money being injected into particular programs. Therefore, in the contributions for direct job creation in this country there is actually a decrease from the forecast expenditure for 1983-84. When the amount is compared to the 1984-85 Estimates, there is actually a decrease of some $219 million in contributions for direct job creation. While the Government says one thing, the actual facts dictate that something else is going on.
What is happening? Is the Government hiding the fact that it had to spend more money in job creation last year? I think not, because I would have applauded it if it had put more into job creation in this country. I rather suspect that the Government is accepting the fact that it is not willing to do anything for the millions of unemployed people in Canada.
The amount forecast to be spent in the 1983-84 Estimates is around $854 million. The Government is not increasing that amount in this Budget but decreasing it. This year's Estimates show only $634 million. It is a shame that the Government will not at least meet the level of spending on job creation that it spent the previous year. It does not speak very highly of the Government, and Canadians will certainly judge it when they go to the polls at the next election.
The Government can create employment in this country by other means than give-aways to big corporate entities in this country, as I think will likely happen. The Member for Comox-Powell River (Mr. Skelly) is more knowledgeable in this area than I am as he is our energy critic. However, the Petroleum Incentives Program is being increased by some $450 million in the 1984-85 Estimates. My concern with this program is that it has no cost control, no job-creation guarantees or performance guarantees. It is another example of the Government's lack of wisdom in offering the larger and sometimes multinational corporations in this country money in the hope that it will trickle down to those who are unemployed and at the bottom of the economic ladder.
I suggest that the Government would be more prudent to use the money that is being given away under the Petroleum Incentives Program for such things as renewable resources and conservation. These two areas are much more labour intensive than the Petroleum Incentives Program which is capital intensive and does not provide any assurance of job creation in this country.
When talking about the money spent on unemployment, the Minister said that it is "a reflection of our improving economic circumstances and the improvement of our level of employment in particular". Nowhere in the Estimates does it show that the economy for the unemployed and those who are in fear of losing their jobs will get any better. As the Leader of the NDP has pointed out, while there is a recovery, it is unfair because those at the upper end of our economic scale, such as

February 21, 1984
Main Estimates, 1984-85
the banks and big corporations, have done quite well while those at the lower end of the socio-economic scale must pay the price. These Estimates make that clear and do nothing to reverse that situation.
We see that Established Programs Financing is being increased by 8 per cent. While the Government often says that it is keeping pace with the times in terms of the money it is contributing to medicare and post-secondary education, it is not so. One need only look at the Bill which was recently passed that put the six and five program into effect on funding to post-secondary level education. It really means that there will be a decrease in excess of $100 million to post-secondary education in this country.
The Government has changed revenue guarantees so that there are no longer revenue guarantees in this country. Almost all of the provinces criticized the federal Government for not keeping pace with Established Programs Financing and, based on the facts, I would have to agree with those provinces. The Government is not doing its share in Established Programs Financing.
There are areas to which the Government has paid lip service. A small item in the Estimates but still very important is the Canadian Centre for Occupational Health and Safety. It was given a 4 per cent increase when the Government promised great rewards for working Canadians through the Canadian Centre for Occupational Health and Safety. In fact, there will even be a loss of nine person-years of employment there.
The Department of Employment and Immigration should be dealing with the overall problem of unemployment and job opportunities in the country. While I applaud the Department and the federal Government for establishing the Ministry of Youth and the Youth Opportunity Fund, I hope further steps will be taken once they are firmly established. We cannot be too critical of a ministry at this time because it does not appear in the 1984-85 Estimates. I assume supplementary estimates will be introduced for the approval of expenditures for the new Youth Ministry.
At the same time that the Government is at least paying lip service to the unemployed youth of this country, it seems to me that it has almost forgotten about natives. The Government does not even survey natives in the unemployment statistics. The 17 reserves in my riding of The Battlefords-Meadow Lake are not reflected in Canada's unemployment statistics. Nothing significant has been done to increase their standard of living in over 100 years since treaties have been signed. Their situation has probably become even worse. I encourage the Government to devise more constructive programs in terms of the settlement of land entitlement and the building of an economic base for native people in Canada.
Another area about which I am somewhat distressed is the unemployment of women. Women and natives seem to be forgotten. While the Government has placed an emphasis on youth employment, it has forgotten about those other two sectors.
I wish to say a few words about the Special Capital Recovery Projects program which has been espoused by the Government for creating jobs and economic opportunities in this country. I believe it is deceiving because the fact is that the Special Capital Recovery Projects program is destroying jobs, as various government departments and agencies now show in these Estimates. Let us take the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, for example. It is receiving an increase of some $75.7 million for higher salaries and for operating capital expenditures. Also under the Special Recovery Capital Projects, it is getting almost $20 million for the purchase of "high technology equipment". As a result, there will be a loss of about 150 person-years of employment resulting from reorganization. I want to ask the President of the Treasury Board whether he is going to assure Canadians that that $20 million is being spent under the Special Recovery Capital Projects in the CBC and whether that money is going to Canadian producers of high technology, and that the CBC will not again take away Canadian jobs by buying foreign high-tech.
I would like to say that when we look at areas that are vitally important to Canadians at present we find some erosion. I understand the Government is limited in terms of what it can do because of the high deficits. In fact, the Hon. Member for Hamilton Mountain (Mr. Deans) mentioned to me in conversation today that if this Government would stop its corporate give-aways and if it would stop the breaks which large corporations do not really need, we could likely save about $10 billion in these Estimates, money which could be put or redirected into employment creation measures.
Let us look at the Department of the Environment. I think its priority would be in terms of protecting our environment from the ravages of industry and neglect by much of the Canadian population. There is one area that has shown a decrease in the Department of the Environment, a decrease of $2.5 million for the toxic chemicals management program. That is a shame, especially when you think of people who live around the Love Canal and those who have to worry about chemical factories and plants. This is a vitally important program. At a time when the Government should be increasing its watch over the environment because of the way we have allowed the environment to be devastated, why is the Government taking away $2.5 million from this most vital program to Canadians?
There is another area on which I want to comment. We have just had a preliminary look through the Estimates. I looked at the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation. That Corporation should be the impetus for building better and more housing right across this land. But what do I see? I see a decrease of $124 million due to the termination of the Canadian Home Ownership Stimulation Plan, a decrease in phasing out neighbourhood improvement programs, community service contributions, loans, investment and advances, including reduced activity in the Canada Rental Supply Plan and a revised cash flow for other plans. If some of the money could be directed into these programs, it would not only help
February 21, 1984

Canadians to get the housing they require but it would also be a spur to the creation of many jobs from the forest industry to the construction material area. Many more jobs would be created by putting more money into the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation to direct that Corporation to build more houses on the basis of need.
Before my time runs out, I want to speak about the Department of Transport. Through Bill C-155, the statutory Crow rate was abolished. We in the New Democratic Party believe that the Crow rate should be reinstated. That program took away from the grain producers in the prairie provinces in western Canada a potential of about $1 billion a year. In the background papers we find an increase of $11 million for western transportation in industrial development initiatives. Behind that we see in brackets "Crow". It is not a very fair deal, Mr. Speaker, when you take from the producers of the western prairie provinces $1 billion and in return show an increase of $11 million for western transportation. That does not seem to be a very fair deal.
At the same time let us look at air strips, which come under the jurisdiction of the Department of Transport, specifically in northern Quebec and Labrador. There will be money for that purpose under the Special Recovery Capital Projects program channelled through the Department of Transport for some $5 million. That seems unfair, too. Do we take away from the transportation system in western Canada in terms of rail transport and augment air transport in other parts of the country? I applaud the Government for improving transportation services in parts of northern Canada, but I do not think it should be at the cost of transportation to Canadians in other vital sectors of our economy, such as in agriculture and in the prairie provinces.
I hope that the Special Recovery Capital Projects program is not all allocated in these Estimates. I hope there is still some room for negotiation with this Government. However, I do see a great deal of that money already allocated in the 1984-85 Estimates. On much of this I do not think that Members of Parliament have had a chance to give input or opinion. I hope the Government will consult with Members of Parliament in the Opposition because I think we understand at least our own constituencies much better than someone else who does not represent the West. We represent western Canada in this particular case, Mr. Speaker. I would value the chance to give opinions on the development of transportation as well as on other vital sectors of our economy in the West.
I see my time is running out. I understand there will be time for questions. I look forward to the opportunity to ask questions of the President of the Treasury Board along with members of the New Democratic Party. I look forward to receiving an explanation to some of the things that we think are lacking in the 1984-85 Estimates.

subtopic: EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF TREASURY BOARD

subtopic: EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF TREASURY BOARD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Estimates reflect spendings on the Petroleum Incentives Program, which ranged in 1982-83 from $1,808 billion to a projected $1,634 billion in 1983-84 and $1.6 billion in 1984-85. The Minister mentioned that those are among some of the largest expenditures in the Estimates. The total value of that program until 1984-85 will be $5,042 billion, about half of which appears to have been invested in the Beaufort Sea area. The Japanese Government has indicated that it was removing itself from this particular operation in the Beaufort Sea because there was no chance of striking oil in the area, and the Estimates indicate that we have invested an enormous amount of money, about $2.2 billion, and will continue to do so. Certainly there are numerous other projects

February 21, 1984
Main Estimates, 1984-85
related to that company's involvement, such as the LNG one at Prince Rupert which there is talk about cancelling.
Given the fact that the Japanese, based on data which they have from Dome Petroleum, have reached the conclusion that there is no oil to be found there, will the Government continue to comply with program criteria in order to have authority to spend these enormous amounts of dollars that are now being spent in a manner which does not or should not comply with program criteria?

subtopic: EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF TREASURY BOARD
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, this program is not limited to assistance to Dome Petroleum for its exploration and development activities in the Beaufort Sea. It also goes to support exploration and development in the Sable Island area, offshore of Nova Scotia.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subtopic: EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF TREASURY BOARD
speechtext: And, you hope, to ship building.

subtopic: EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF TREASURY BOARD
speechtext:
It goes to support exploration and development activities offshore of Newfoundland. It goes to support exploration and development activities throughout Canada, to companies which meet the criteria. By the way, these are primarily Canadian companies.
As my hon. friend on the other side of the House points out, money spent under this program for exploration and development goes indirectly toward supporting activities by other sectors such as the Canadian shipbuilding sector for supply vessels, rigs and those sorts of things. Even with respect to the Beaufort Sea, we are not talking only about Dome. We are talking about other companies like Esso, Gulf and Petro-Canada. Therefore, I do not think it would be fair to suggest that, whatever is the situation with respect to Dome, this particular program is not as valuable and useful as I think it is for the Canadian economy. Certainly, as I understand the program, money is spent as exploration and development work is carried out. If there are companies which do less exploration and development work, obviously they receive less funds from the program. This is something which I am sure the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Chretien) would be very pleased to explore in detail with my hon. friend when he appears before the relevant parliamentary committee which will be studying the Estimates.
I would say that the program has proven itself and will continue to prove itself to be a very valuable way of assisting the overall development of the Canadian economy, particularly the resource sectors, by encouraging exploration and development primarily of Canadian companies. I do not know why my hon. friend has become so conservative that he seems to be opposing exploration activities by Canadian companies.

subtopic: EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF TREASURY BOARD
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I believe the Minister mentioned that it was one of the eight largest expenditures in the Budget. I wish my colleague in the Conservative Party would recognize that it is his Party which is holding up legislation that might in fact improve shipbuilding.

subtopic: EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF TREASURY BOARD
speechtext: Nonsense, absolute nonsense.

subtopic: EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF TREASURY BOARD
speechtext:
We all know that an enormous amount of shipbuilding has gone offshore. I challenge the Minister to name a rig working in the Beaufort Sea which was built in Canada. Be that as it may, I return to the fact that there is no time to explore this with the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Chretien). There is barely enough time for the House to explore the question. I believe, as do many other people, that the country will be damaged if in fact the company with which we are dealing today and which is taking roughly half these expenditures goes down the drain.
With the announcement of the Japanese today, and in view of the fact that Dome owes roughly $4.2 billion to the Canadian and American consortium of banks and that Citicorp which is owed $1.4 billion is demanding payment now, it could easily be that the company would fold up before the House or the committee has had a chance to consider it. It is important for many aspects of the Canadian economy, for many industries and suppliers, that we should deal with it now. It would be very helpful if the Minister could indicate whether or not the Government intends to continue spending those horrendous amounts of PIP dollars. Does the Government intend to put up the $500 million to bail out Dome? Just exactly what are we bailing it out for, when the Japanese say that there is no oil at the bottom of the Beaufort Sea, when they are prepared to walk away and leave a half billion dollar investment and to shut down an LNG project on the West Coast because they do not believe Dome has the financial strength to invest in the program and bring it to completion? What is going through the minds of the other creditors of Dome, the Canadian and American banks? If they call Dome and it goes into insolvency, what happens to Canada? What happens to the Davie shipyard? What happens to the mines and the conventional activities of Dome? The question is so serious that it is the time to deal with it now. It is time the Minister told the House whether they are complying with program requirements to take up additional billions of dollars. If they are not, perhaps we should look hard at ways of spending those additional dollars in ways which would be more helpful to Canadians, perhaps along the lines of the Japanese. It is a cut bait and run situation.

subtopic: EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF TREASURY BOARD
speechtext:
I am delighted to note the calls of the Hon. Member for a massive rescue operation for Dome. His hon. friend, in responding to my statement on the Estimates, complained about alleged excessive support for big companies. My hon. friend seems to be calling for a massive move to rescue a big company. I would be happy to bring his representations to the attention of the Minister of Finance and to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources.
Of course we hope there will be consideration, if necessary, of such a step for which my hon. friend is calling. He is an unusual friend of big business, nevertheless we have to take his comments seriously as an Hon. Member of the House and bring them to the attention of the appropriate Ministers. However, I want to stress that the Petroleum Incentives Program grants are not limited to Dome. They are available to companies operating offshore in the Atlantic, in other frontier
February 21, 1984

areas and throughout Canada. The expenditure of money by the Government will have to be based upon the approval of these Estimates by Parliament and, more than that, following upon the terms and conditions of legislation adopted by the House. As far as 1 am aware, the Department has a considerable staff whose job it is to ensure that the terms and conditions are being met. If my hon. friend has any facts to indicate the opposite, certainly the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources and I would be very happy to have that information.
In any event, if the firms in question are not meeting the eligibility requirements for this money, then, even if it is provided for in the Estimates, it will not be spent, and there will be a lapse in these funds and this will be reflected in the Financial situation at the end of the fiscal year. In conclusion, even though it comes from a most unlikely source, this anguished plea for the immediate rescue of a very large business, I will bring it promptly to the attention of the Minister of Finance and of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. The Minister should stop misleading the House. He knows that we called for not one more-

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, last year the Minister had a central reserve in the Estimates of $900 million. This year he has reduced the central reserve to $800 million, even though he has dramatically increased the estimated expenditure by over 10.4 per cent. Why is the central reserve reduced when the total amount proposed to be spent is dramatically higher? The normal practice was to have a central reserve in excess of 1 per cent of the spending. This is now down to .8 per cent of anticipated spending. Is this just to pretend that budget figures will not be as much in the hole as they will in fact turn out to be?

subtopic: EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF TREASURY BOARD
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the proposal for the size of the central reserve is based on a careful assessment by officials of its possible use to fund programs pending the necessity of dealing with them in supplementary estimates and the other usual purposes. I thought my hon. friend would welcome this type of effort at restraint. I will check this with my officials in the light of his comments. Certainly if there are grounds for having a higher central reserve, I will be happy to bring this proposal to the attention of the Minister of Finance and Cabinet.

subtopic: EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF TREASURY BOARD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister will know that including the central reserve last year, he had a reserve against program envelopes of $2.4 billion, for a total reserve including the central reserve of $3.3 billion. He has thus far broken out $5,763 billion in his Estimates. In other words, he did not have
Main Estimates, 1984-85
enough reserves last year by $2.4 billion, yet this year he reduces his reserves and pretends that he will not have any supps and that he will not break those reserve limits. Why will the Minister not come clean with the House right now? Realizing that supplementary estimates have invariably spent $5 billion to $6 billion, why will he not make those kinds of reserves in this budget and in his estimates when he prepares them in the first place? Let's not keep kidding people.

subtopic: EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF TREASURY BOARD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as far as I am aware, the envelope figures in question have been sufficient to accommodate supplementary estimates. Obviously if the Minister of Finance provides a revised fiscal framework and adjusts the envelopes, that is something that has to be considered subsequent to the tabling of main estimates. Unlike last year when the Main Estimates preceded the Budget, in this case we have a return to the more traditional approach where the Budget presented by the Minister of Finance has preceded the tabling of Main Estimates. I am glad my hon. friend has noted that obviously our total outlay and the framework it represents has to have room in it for supplementary estimates. That is why we have a figure for envelope reserves. As far as I am aware, we have not presented to the House in the past since setting up this envelope system, and it is an action which has been shared with the preceding government, offered supplementary estimates in excess of the fiscal framework stipulated by the Minister of Finance. I will certainly note his point. As far as I am aware, we have been consistent with the concept of the envelope system, including having supplementary estimates presented to the House when required which fit in within the envelope reserve figure.
I want to add, with respect to the Hon. Member's interesting question about the central reserve, that it does reflect a point I made in my statement, that is, that the Main Estimates do reflect a more optimistic view which the Government shares with the private sector about the state of the economy. The size of the central reserve as a result reflects that, anticipating there will not be some of the same kinds of demands on it as was the case last year when the economy was just beginning to enter into the phase of recovery.

February 21, 1984
Main Estimates, 1984-85

Member for Mississauga South making a very big point last year that we were allegedly not basing our comparison on main estimates to main estimates. It is also valid as part of the overall study of the issue to compare total forecast expenditure with what is in these estimates. I am sorry I am not able to calculate a percentage in my head on the spot, but if one takes the figures in the Estimates that I just tabled for job creation and add to that $150 million additional from the Budget for the Youth Opportunity Fund and the close to $1 billion to be spent this coming fiscal year for the Special Recovery Capital Projects, one will certainly have a figure for assistance for the creation of jobs through fairly direct activity by the federal Government which will exceed by a respectable amount, to say the least, what is forecast with respect to 1983-84.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subtopic: EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF TREASURY BOARD
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, a short while ago the Minister alluded to the fact that the PIP grants, the structure and the system, encourage and lend support to the Canadian shipbuilding industry. The Minister might want to correct that. Recently a Newfoundland company ordered two fairly large and quite expensive offshore anchor and supply rigs from a company in Korea. It did so because it becomes a cost, and cost is part of the formula under which PIP picks it up. In the preparation of the Estimates, did the President of the Treasury Board consider the impact of the PIP grants as presently constituted on the Canadian shipbuilding industry? Did he consider their impact on temporary input of foreign vessels for offshore work, particularly on the East Coast? Was that impact fully considered by his officials and officials in the Ministry of Finance and the Ministry of Energy? On reflection, the Minister might want to agree that PIP grants, as constituted with respect to construction of offshore vessels and rigs with respect to temporary import duties or full duties that are paid on foreign registered ships operating in Canadian waters, are in fact detrimental and not as he suggested?

subtopic: EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF TREASURY BOARD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend has raised a useful point. One of the reasons I made the comment in answer to a question raised by a colleague earlier was that I thought he was encouraging me to link the operation of the PIP grants to the Canadian shipbuilding industry in a favourable way. In fact he is saying that I misunderstood his comment whispered across the floor of the House. If that is so, I will be happy to look into the matter further.
It is my impression that there is more money being spent in Canada for goods, materials and equipment than would otherwise be the case if there were no PIP grants and the resulting encouragement of exploration and development by oil companies. I think that could certainly be demonstrated.
With respect to the vessels that my hon. friend has said would be constructed in Korea, I would be interested in knowing what degree of Canadian content there is in these vessels, machinery, equipment and so on. I would not be surprised if, even though the vessels are built in Korea and the hulls are made there, there would not be some respectable degree of Canadian equipment.
I think I am right in my overall assertion that a lot more is being spent in Canada, not only for salaries and wages for Canadian workers, but also for machinery, equipment and other things than would be the case if we did not have the PIP program with the resulting favourable effect on exploration and development of oil and gas in Canadian territorial waters and on land in Canada.
I will be happy to examine my hon. friend's question further because he raises an interesting point. I should like to observe, however, that if there is a problem, it would seem to me that the solution lies not so much in the structure of the PIP program but in the operation of our temporary duty system, rules for coasting vessels and that sort of thing.
