speakeroldname: Hon. Flora MacDonald (Kingston and the Islands):
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have seen the Government raise the art of deception to new levels in recent days but I do not suppose it ever surpassed its efforts as it did the other day when the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) brought down his Budget. He called this document a program of action. As far as most Canadians are concerned, I can tell him that it is a non-event, a non-starter that is going nowhere, a vehicle that ran out of steam before it ever got started.
How can one consider that the Budget is anything but a non-event? Does it do anything at all for the unemployed? The answer is no. Does it do anything for the national debt? Again the answer is no. Does it do anything for the deficit, for research and development or for investment? To all of these vital questions which lie at the very heart of any endeavour to achieve economic recovery in the country, the answer again and again is no.
I believe that this so-called Budget is little more than an apology to the people of Canada by the Government for the admission of failure, which it surely is. It is an apology for the
Government's inability to exercise either Fiscal responsibility or moral authority at a critical time in the country's history.
If you read it you will see that it apologizes to small business for the hopeless mess it made of the tax system. It apologizes to taxpayers for the abuses it has permitted in the Department of National Revenue. It continues to apologize to the oil and gas industry for the massive damage the National Energy Program has done to that industry. That program was introduced by the Minister of Finance in a previous existence. This morning the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) stood in her place and apologized because the supposed pension reforms were so very limited, as well she might. However, as with many apologies, the Minister's Budget presentation is also self-serving. Mitigating circumstances are presented as virtues and promises to do better in the future and heralded as if they were already a fait accompli. "We will have 5 per cent growth this year," the Minister declares. "We will reduce unemployment to 7.5 per cent by 1988. The deficit will fall next year or perhaps the year after or the year after that". However, Sir, what I would like to ask the Minister is, what do all these brave forecasts and future expectations give Canadians today? What good does talking about tomorrow do for someone who has lost his or her job more than a year ago and has no more hope of finding a job today than he or she did then? What good is $150 million in youth employment funds when it works out to $5 per person per week? What good is mortgage insurance to those thousands who have already lost their homes?
For our part, we welcome mortgage insurance. It was, after all, the cornerstone of the Budget which was introduced by my colleague, the Hon. Member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie), back in 1979. That, Mr. Speaker, was the only innovative, responsive and responsible Budget to be presented to this House in a good many years, and what happened to it? It was rejected by the Liberal Party and the New Democratic Party combined. This Party offered mortgage insurance more than four years ago when it would really have helped thousands of Canadians to keep their homes through the recession. This Government has had four years since then in which to introduce such insurance, but it only brings it out now when, according to the Minister of Finance the danger is over. Why that lengthy wait?
This non-budget, this non-event, must be judged a failure by any standard. The Minister had the opportunity to take decisive action, to give Canadians concrete proposals, and he fluffed it, he blew it, and nowhere is his failure more apparent than in his response to the question of pension reform. Four years ago, Mr. Speaker, this Government announced that pension reform was to be one of its key priorities. For three years we waited and waited. Finally, we received the green paper which was released by the Minister of National Health and Welfare and subsequently this House authorized a parliamentary task force to hold hearings and make recommendations on pension reform. Now, in the last weeks and months of a Parliament which has already surpassed the normal time
February 21, 1984

period of any legitimate Parliament, in the final weeks and months of the term of this body, the Minister of Finance has taken the first faltering steps toward the implementation of reform and, as usual, he has missed the mark once again. Fie declared in the House last Wednesday when he was presenting his Budget measure, "The Government will never turn its back on those who spend their working lives helping to build this country and who now need help themselves". Never turn its back on that group of people? Never, Mr. Speaker? Then why is it that we have right now in this country more than 600,000 Canadians over the age of 65 who are living in poverty? The $50 a month increase in the guaranteed income supplement will be welcome, make no mistake, even if its recipients have to wait another 10 months before they get the total amount. Why do they have to wait 10 months? That has not been explained, and was not explained this morning by the Minister of National Health and Welfare when she spoke. However, I would say to you, Sir, that a $50 increase is not a solution to the problem of poverty or of pension reform.
The parliamentary task force recommended an immediate increase-not an increase 10 months down the road-of $102 a month for those most in need. The $50 proposed increase will still leave single pensioners who rely entirely on the old age pension and the guaranteed income supplement almost $2,000 below the poverty line in any medium-sized city across this country.
Certainly, anyone in this House would agree with the proposals to amend the Pension Benefits Standards Act to ensure that survivor benefits will no longer be cut off if the recipient remarries. We all agree with having pension credits split equally between spouses on marriage breakdown and at age 65. Those proposals are not contentious. They have been around for a long time. Hon. Members on all sides of the House have been advocating that something be done about them. They could have been introduced many budgets ago if the Minister of Finance had wanted to do so, but he did not. However, he has finally come forward with them now. His only claim to merit in bringing in these proposals is that he has seen fit not to overlook them once again. But where the Minister cannot lay any claim to merit of any kind, Sir, is in virtually all of the other proposals with regard to pension reform. These proposals fly in the face of not only the task force recommendation but particularly the recommendations by the many women's groups and organizations which appeared before the parliamentary task force.
One of the witnesses before that parliamentary task force was, of course, the Minister of National Health and Welfare. She came before the task force on March 17, 1983, almost a year ago, Mr. Speaker. The evidence which she gave presumably reflected not only her own opinion, but surely that of her Department, the Government, and the Cabinet of which she is a member. Last March she said, and I quote:
1 believe coverage is the key issue of pension reform. I really mean extension of coverage to all workers, and that is on a universal basis. That is what I mean.
The Budget-Miss MacDonald
She went on:
You see, the majority of working Canadians do not belong to private pension plans. Only 54 per cent of men and 38 per cent of women in paid employment are protected by a private pension plan. These are cold, hard facts.
Those are the words of the Minister, Mr. Speaker, "Cold, hard facts". I would say to her that they are made all the colder by her colleague, the Minister of Finance. This Budget does nothing, absolutely nothing, to further the key issue which the Minister declared, which, as we all know, is the issue of coverage. The Minister may well schedule discussions with her provincial counterparts at a later date-who knows when-to explore the introduction of the homemaker's pension under the Canada-Quebec Pension Plan. I am very aware that it is an item which needs to have the approval of two-thirds of the provinces with two-thirds of the population. However, it is not enough, Sir, for the federal Government to simply put it on the agenda. The federal Government has to become the advocate of that plan. A commitment to discussion, Sir? Discussions on this issue have been going on since 1970 when it was a recommendation of the Royal Commission on the Status of Women. A commitment to discussion surely is not enough for the millions of Canadian women who work in the home and contribute as much as those in the paid labour force to the wellbeing of our society. They want to be sure that the Minister of National Health and Welfare, and her colleague, the Minister of Finance, will be fighting on their behalf to have the Canada-Quebec Pension Plan extended to homemakers. But there is absolutely nothing which gives that guarantee.
The insistence of women on this particular issue was very well documented by the National Action Committee on the Status of Women. On January 16 of this year, prior to the Budget proposals, they wrote to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) and sent me and other members of the Parliamentary Task Force a copy of the letter. In it they said:
Thousands of women have expressed to us their dislike of the present treatment of homemakers in the Canada-Quebec Pension Plan, and of the inadequacy of the green paper recommendations in that regard. Most women are full or part-time homemakers want to be recognized as workers and be entitled to pensions in their own right. They do not trust widows pensions that are based on their husband's income and that disappear if the marriage ends in divorce. Therefore, we strongly urge you to support the task force's proposals which will grant homemakers direct coverage under the Canada Quebec Pension Plan.
That, Sir, came from the largest umbrella organization covering women's groups in this country. The right to pension coverage for the people of whom they are speaking, the homemakers, was not addressed. A few simple words in the Budget was all it would have taken to give encouragement to these people that the Government recognizes their work and their achievements in their own right. Let me suggest to the Minister of Finance what those words might have been. He might have said: We fully support the full concept of homemakers pensions and we want to do all we can to introduce them. That is all it would have taken, but it was not done.
There is another major part of the pension proposals I want to address, Mr. Speaker. I know my time is limited, but it concerns the way in which the Government has gone about

February 21, 1984
The Budget-Miss MacDonald
addressing RRSPs. Increasing the limits of RRSPs will surely not help the 46 per cent of male and 62 per cent of female workers in the paid labour force who presently have no private coverage. It may help those who can afford to put $10,000 a year in such plans and I am sure it will be welcomed by those who are earning in excess of $55,000 a year. But what about the 94 per cent of Canadian wage earners who do not earn $55,000? In particular, what about the great majority of Canadians who earn less than $30,500 a year and who will not benefit by one penny from this $300 million exercise in largesse by the Minister? They are ignored and forgotten, Sir. There is not even an indication of a concept in this Budget to provide the means of private pension coverage to the many Canadians who earn between $10,000 and $30,000 a year. But that is an issue which the parliamentary task force did address. It put forward a very simple proposal for a straightforward 40 per cent tax credit which would have allowed many of these workers, particularly women, to achieve private pension plans.
This Budget and the pension proposals in it show that the Government has its priorities all wrong. It provides an extra $300 million in benefits for those who already have pension coverage, while at the same time completely ignoring homemakers as well as low and middle income workers who have no pension coverage other than the Canada Pension Plan. It particularly ignores the plight of the many thousands, mostly women, who find themselves in the lost age bracket between 60 and 65 who have little or no income, have lost their spouses, yet are ineligible for pension. The $300 million the Minister is giving to those with incomes in excess of $55,000 a year would more than provide pensions for that group of persons. But the Minister would not turn his attention to those people and neither would the Minister of National Health and Welfare.

-with policy priorities and credibility from the Tories. I would like to ask the Hon. Member for Kingston and the Islands about her policies and priorities and where they fit in the general credibility of the Tory Party.
As I look across the aisle today, and as Canadians look at the Tory Party, we see the Hon. Member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) in the ascendancy. We see the Hon. Member for York-Peel (Mr. Stevens) is still a very strong voice. The Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn) is a strong voice. All of them are arguing cut, cut, cut. The services we provide to people are the things they are going to cut.
What services and priorities would a "mean, nasty, tough-minded" Minister of Finance in the Tory Party cut? I would like to hear some priorities among people rather than the usual propaganda we get from the other side.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am so pleased to be asked this question. I can tell the Hon. Member that there are three priorities in the social field that this Party and its Leader have stated. We only wish the Government would wake up to them.
One happens to be jobs for people who are unemployed so they can begin to get back their self dignity and begin to be contributing and productive members in the economy and pay revenues into the Government.
Another social program which we have said would receive much more attention than the limited Bill which the Minister has put forward, is the reform of the health care system in the country. This is vitally needed by people who cannot get into hospitals and by hospitals for which there is no capital funding.
The third issue, which we have been addressing continually, is in the field of pension reform. We have been asking for it for the last four years throughout the life of the Government. We raised questions three years ago, two years ago and a year ago with the Minister of Finance. We asked where the funding was for the people over the age of 65 living below the poverty line. Every time that question was raised, the Minister of Finance or the Minister of Health and Welfare got up in the House, and said, "We will do it when the resources permit". Two years ago they told the elderly of the country they could not have any increase. They could put it into Canadair, Petro-Canada or Petrofina or any other thing, but could not give it to the elderly people of the country. Now, just before an election, they have suddenly discovered they can do something. The elderly people know that the priorities of this Party have long been to improve their position.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before I begin I will say that I am going to turn some of my remarks in the latter part of my speech to the issues raised by the Member for
The Budget-Mr. Frith
Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald) vis-a-vis the Government's commitment to pension reform, and I would like to answer some of the questions she has raised.
First, I would like to begin where the Hon. Member for Kingston and the Islands left off. She said that the priority of her Party is today's elderly. The only way in which I can determine what kind of commitment the Conservative Party actually has to the elderly in the country is to go back to the 1979 Budget for which it was responsible. At the time, the Hon. Member for Kingston and the Islands said that that was one of the better budgets introduced in the country in years. Looking back at that 1979 Budget to discover what moneys were allocated for the guaranteed income supplement, I see the answer is, zero. The only year in which we can judge the treatment of the elderly people in this nation by the Conservative Party is 1979. Not one extra dollar in that Budget was allocated for the guaranteed income supplement.
The Member for Kingston and the Islands knows that part of the election platform of the Liberal Party in 1980 was a commitment to increase the guaranteed income supplement by $35. I would like to remind the Hon. Member for Kingston and the Islands that that commitment was met within the first six months of the Government's taking office. Since that time, through this Budget, we have allocated a further $460 million to the poorest in our society. I am not sure the Member for Kingston and the Islands has any idea what her colleague, the Hon. Member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie), has in mind for the elderly in the country.
The Hon. Member for St. John's West has consistently asked what the priorities of the Government are. A budget is a number of things, but in essence it is a blueprint which outlines the government's commitment to certain sectors of our population and economy. When one looks at the Budget which was tabled last week we see that the Government wants to increase the moneys being made available for today's elderly by $460 million. We recognize that we have a tremendous unemployment problem in the country, largely with the youth. We have allocated $150 million in addition to the $500 million that was allocated in the 1983-84 Budget. This was specifically designed to alleviate the problems of the unemployed youth in the country.
Yet when the Hon. Member for St. John's West commented on behalf of his Party about the priorities of the Government, he focused on the fact that we had done nothing to alleviate the problem of the federal deficit. All his remarks were based on reducing the size of the deficit. If in fact 75 per cent of our moneys go out in transfer payments and on the public debt, that leaves only 25 per cent on which I assume he is going to do some drastic cutting. I do not know what the Hon. Member for St. John's West means when he says he wants to have a substantial reduction in the size of the federal deficit. I assume it must mean $5 billion to $7 billion. Let us examine some ways in which we could reduce the size of the deficit by that amount. Is it going to occur in the $10.4 billion that is spent on pensions for the elderly? I doubt that very much. Is it the position of the Conservative Party that it is going to cut into

February 21, 1984
The Budget-Mr. Frith
the pensions of the elderly? Is it going to cut off the $2.3 billion in family allowance? Is that the position of the Conservative Party? Is it going to cut into the equalization payments from the federal Government to the provinces? The Conservatives say they want to put more money into medicare and the care of the elderly. If I understood the Conservative defence critic and foreign affairs critic properly, the Conservatives' position is that they want even more money in the Budget to deal with increased moneys spent on defence. If I am not mistaken, the Finance critic for the Conservative Party has said he would favour a removal of the Canadian ownership special charge, which brought in some $700 million in the last fiscal year.
Clearly, when I listen to the Conservative Party, I have difficulty in understanding exactly what their policies are. If the Tories want a reduction in the deficit, they had better start telling the Canadian people where they will make the cuts. I suggest that they should realize that as a Party they are afraid to tell the Canadian people what those cuts would be. They are afraid of the repercussions if they told the elderly that they wanted to cut back on pensions. They are afraid to tell Canadians that there will be less money for medicare. They are afraid to tell the Canadian public that there will be less money for post-secondary education. Those are the answers Canadians are looking for, but not from us because we have clearly stated that we are on theside of the elderly and on the side of the poor and that we intend to maintain our commitments to the provinces.
That is not the position of the Conservative Party. In this year that precedes the next general election, I suggest that Canadians should have an idea of the policies that the Conservative Party will favour before Canadians make a decision.
The Hon. Member for Kingston and the Islands asked about the federal commitment to pension reform. She said that evidently our commitment is not as strong as our words and that we are finally getting around to pension reform in our budget document. She suggested that the Conservative Party asked for that type of pension reform two years ago and that in effect there already was a commitment to the need for pension reform in the nation. The Hon. Member must know, having been a member of the special task force on pension reform that there was no consensus. That is precisely why the federal Government led to the formation of a parliamentary task force in order to travel throughout the country to determine where the consensus was before we could act.
I noticed that the Member for Kingston and the Islands suggested that the improvements to the Canada Pension Plan are long overdue. While I agree with her, I would point out to her that federal Conservative policy cannot be separated from provincial Conservative policy. In that respect the party that I would blame the most for blocking some of the needed improvements to the Canada Pension Plan is the Conservative Party. It was not the federal Government. I recall two years
ago when the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) attended a joint conference with her provincial counterparts at which she suggested an immediate doubling of Canada Pension Plan disability payments. We were told at the time by the Treasurer of Ontario that he was totally opposed to any increase in the amount of Canada Pension Plan disability payments that were going to be made.
The Member for Kingston and the Islands knows full well that any changes to the Canada Pension Plan require approval of two-thirds of the provinces representing two-thirds of the population. In effect, Ontario has a veto power, because of the size of its population, on changes to the Canada Pension Plan. The Conservative Party of Ontario effectively used that veto power to stop the child drop-out provision in this country which we have been advocating for years. The Tories opposed it. We have been advocating the doubling of the Canada Pension Plan disability payment, and the Tories of Ontario have opposed it.
If we want to find a Party in this country which is inhibiting or blocking pension reform, I suggest that she look to her own Province of Ontario and begin to talk to the Conservatives at Queen's Park to have them come on side with the federal Liberals. We might then get pension reform much quicker.
I want to deal with equality and the fact that the Budget pays a great deal of attention to a comprehensive lifetime limit. I am not sure if the Member for Kingston and the Islands represents the points of view of her Party, but with respect to the increases in the amounts of money that will be allowed for tax deductible purposes, that is the increase in the Registered Retirement Savings Plan which is an integral part of pension reform in this country, that concept of a comprehensive lifetime limit introduces a degree of flexibility in the pension system that was never there before. It introduces a degree of equality in the system which was never there before.
She knows full well that the tax treatment with respect to pension plans for several groups in our society has not been equal. Surely the Member is not suggesting that she will defend on behalf of her Party the exclusion of equality for small business people in this country, and for farmers who desperately need that equality. This provision for equality of tax treatment improves that situation. It improves tax assistance for the self-employed in this country. These are all people for whom she has a great deal of concern.
The comprehensive lifetime limit provides equality to those people who, of their own volition, have no access to a private pension plan in their own name, and it also introduces a degree of equality to those people which has not been in the system until now. Surely she is not turning her back on the farmers of this country who have been pleading for better tax treatment on capital gains for the sales of their farms.
This Budget of the Minister of Finance will, in effect, remove any taxes payable by a farmer on the first $240,000 on the sale of the farm. Surely she is not opposed to that. We on this side of the House recognize that the small business people in this country are the engine for growth in our economy. Why should they not have the same access to tax assistance and the
February 21, 1984

ability to plan for their future retirement years as we have given to people who have defined benefit plans? Surely she is not arguing that point.
What is her view with respect to self-employed professionals in this country? I know members of the NDP questioned that treatment in some of their remarks. Simply because someone is a lawyer, doctor, dentist or pharmacist, why should they be taxed differently from anyone else in the country? For once we have introduced a tax measure in this Budget that deals fairly with those groups, of which there are many. Frankly, 1 would favour giving even more small breaks to the small business people. We have given $150 million in tax deductions to them in this Budget.
If the Hon. Member recognizes, as we do, that we must give breaks to small business in order to create jobs and make a dent in the high unemployment rates in this country, she will not argue against those tax measures which we have introduced in the Budget.
The comprehensive tax limit introduces for the first time into retirement planning the greatest degree of flexibility possible in any pension system in the western industrialized countries. We are saying that young people in Canada who are raising a family, paying a mortgage but do not have sufficient funds to put aside for retirement purposes will no longer be penalized as they were in the previous system. According to that system, if one could not afford to put money aside for an RRSP, there was no provision for carry-forward. Under the new system, that will be possible for the first time. When a person is finished with his responsibility of caring for a family and paying a mortgage, perhaps when he reaches the age of 50, he will be allowed to have total flexibility in putting aside the carry-forward provision. He can put aside money on his own to better plan for his retirement and put less demand on the state when he hits the age of 65.
If there has been any advocate of pension reform in this country, it has been the Liberal Party. We have established royal commissions on pension reform. We have asked for a national pensions conference, which was not asked for by the Party of the Member for Kingston and the Islands during its short term in office. For them to suggest that there was consensus in this country on the direction of pension reform is doing a disservice to the actual degree of consensus that we did have in the early 1980s on pension reform.
I hope the Member for Kingston and the Islands will support the Budget measures and convince her colleagues not to delay the legislation we are asking for. If we bring in legislation to deal with the Federal Standards Benefits Act, surely there will not be any opposition to the idea of better vesting, a better degree of portability, of two-year vesting or better survivors' benefits. I expect that we should be able to get very quick legislative action with respect to opening the Federal Standards Benefits Act.
I think it is fair to say that the pension issue itself and the report by the parliamentary task force was a very beneficial and unique experience for all members of the committee, regardless of political affiliation. I suggest that the two Oppo-
The Budget-Mr. Frith
sition Parties should pay compliments for the degree of response that was given by the Minister of Finance in his Budget to the recommendations in our report and, in particular to the swiftness of that response. Clearly he recognized that we had a political consensus in the country. I point out 8 of 9 members of that task force signed that report. The only dissenting opinion was given by the New Democratic Party. I would expect, with that degree of consensus, that we can get on with the job of reforming the pension system. For once rather than waiting for the Province of Ontario and other provinces to act, we have decided as a Government to lead by example. Therefore, the opening up of the Federal Standards Benefits Act and the opening up probably of the Public Service Superannuation Act will be a requirement. Surely when we open up the Income Tax Act to reflect the changes outlined in the Budget of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) we will not have any blocking tactics by the Progressive Conservative Party. I hope not. With respect to the commitment by the Hon. Member's Party, I hope that, as the spokesman for her Party, she represents her Party's viewpoints and that the Conservative Party is advocating the inclusion of homemakers in the Canada Pension Plan.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: More than your Party is.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Certainly if you are doing that, you will make it a lot easier for the present Minister of National Health and Welfare to set up negotiations with her provincial counterparts. Let me point out to the Hon. Member for Kingston and the Islands that we now have another treasurer in the Province of Ontario, unfortunately, still a Conservative treasurer. But he has not learned from the experiences of his predecessor, the Hon. Frank Miller, the Member for Muskoka. In a speech just six days ago to the Pension Plan Management Association, he said he was not in favour of two-year vesting; he wants only five years. He is not in favour of including homemakers in the Canada Pension Plan. I would hope that if anyone is advocating the inclusion of homemakers in the Canada Pension Plan, the Hon. Member for Kingston and the Islands after this evening's vote will get on the phone and phone Larry Grossman to tell him that it is a policy area which the federal Conservative Party wants implemented and ask him to stop the opposition to it. If that is the position of the federal Party, I hope that she can convince her provincial counterparts of the need for that kind of inclusion. I wish her luck. We did not have much luck, as I mentioned before. The disabled of this country should realize that because of the veto power in Ontario under the Canada Pension Plan the poorest of the poor, the neediest and the disabled, are deprived of disability benefits. This is the case because Frank Miller for five years has flogged a doubling of the Canada Pension Plan disability.
I ask you as Members of Parliament, what is your greatest problem in your constituencies? I expect you to say it is the people between the ages of 45 and 64 who, through misfortune, have found themselves having to rely solely on Canada Pension Plan disability payments to survive. I think we all

Is it the pleasure of the House to adopt the amendment to the amendment?

speechtext:
There are a lot of things that we are going to be doing for Canadian women that will significantly improve their lot. Better survivor benefits will be introduced. For the first time we are going to mandate a minimum degree of inflation protection. That is something not even the Conservative Government of Ontario advocated until three days ago. I suggest that had it not been for the Minister of Finance and his commitment to pension reform in this Budget, we would not even have the degree of debate and consensus that has developed, such as was demonstrated by the Hon. Larry Grossman in the Province of Ontario who, probably by some fluke, decided on Sunday night to give a speech on pension reform, not knowing that pension reform was going to be an integral part of this Budget. At least we forced the Treasurer of Ontario to a commitment and a degree of commitment to pension reform that until now has not existed in the Province of Ontario. I am glad at least he has gone that far.
Last but not least I want to talk about that degree of inflation protection that we will give to Canadian workers in the private pension plan field. Surely, the Hon. Member for Kingston and the Islands knows that of all the representations we had from across the country the one workers wanted most of all was to have some degree of inflation protection built into the private pension plan system to reflect better the emerging world in which we live and with which we have to cope and deal on a day to day basis.
If the Conservative Party will allow quick passage of all the things we have included in pension reform in this Budget, it will make a much better tomorrow for Canadian workers than we have had until now.
